body:
Solid fundamentals, steady profitability, and resilient occupier demand will be the silver linings in what promises to be another challenging year for European real estate in 2027. Once again, geopolitical headwinds and macroeconomic uncertainty are front of mind, suggesting the industry must wait a while longer to escape its recent inertia.

Now in its 24th edition, the Emerging Trends in Real Estate®: Europe 2027 report is based on a joint survey by PwC and the Urban Land Institute (ULI), providing an in-depth outlook on the real estate market across Europe for the coming year and beyond.

Rising energy and construction costs and higher-for-longer interest rates mean the optimism seen across European real estate in early 2026 has largely dissipated. Industry leaders canvassed for this year’s report point to thin volumes and a pervasive sense of caution, as buyers and sellers wrestle over valuations.

In the background, the industry’s long-term transition continues to play out. This is influenced by a focus on scale, resilience, operational cashflow, and infrastructure. A natural result of those trends is continuing appetite for deal making, with higher-than-average M&A activity set to continue in the year ahead, supported by weak equity market valuations.

The industry’s shifting priorities are evident in the survey’s sector rankings, which reflect a growing focus on energy transition and digital infrastructure. Despite concern over their environmental impact, data centres are seen as significant opportunities, and the industry itself is ramping up its use of AI. Housing affordability has also moved up the agenda. Respondents highlight affordability and supply constraints as the biggest risk to Europe’s long-term economic competitiveness and the most significant social challenge facing the continent over the next decade.

However, even in tough market conditions, there are opportunities. The report highlights the rising influence of family offices and other sources of private capital, which are playing a greater role in the market as some institutional investors remain cautious. Some larger market participants are leaning into their deep resources, with executives telling us that excellent execution and the ability to invest across volatile economic cycles remain a source of competitive advantage.

In an uncertain market, the ability to scale is a powerful competitive advantage, and is the driving force behind a new wave of deal-making. The past year saw significant two-way M&A between the US and Europe, including investment manager Nuveens’ £9.9 billion takeover of Schroders and Prologis’ proposed £14 billion purchase of industrial landlord Segro. In the other direction, Savills in August completed its acquisition of New-York Eastdil Secured for £827 million.

Industry participants see deal making as a direct route to better performance: “The big guys are going to do the best business,” says one institutional investment manager. “They have the best data, the best distribution, and the best people.”

A supporting factor in M&A markets is the persistent discount at which listed property companies trade to their underlying asset values. European listed property companies, including REITs, were trading at an average 37.5% discount to net asset value at the end of September 2026, according to the European Public Real Estate Association (EPRA), well above the 10-year average discount of 21.3%. Discounts were widest in residential (61.8%) - driven largely by the German residential companies, and office (50.6%), and even otherwise favoured sectors were trading well below their longer-term levels: healthcare was at a 24.3% discount and industrial was at 13.9%, against small average premiums to NAV over the past ten years.These conditions have led to opportunistic deals such as CareTrust REIT's 2025 acquisition of Care REIT, at a 9.4% discount to the target's last reported EPRA net tangible assets.

US players such as BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street are making waves, reinforcing both M&A and private capital trends. That said, interviewees point to this changing nature of capital and ownership structures and the wider impact this can have on the industry including asset management strategies, stewardship and ESG.

From a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño to floods in Nepal and wildfires across Europe, the past 12 months have provided further headlines around climate change, a theme explored as a special topic in the past edition of Emerging Trends in Real Estate Europe. But ESG has fallen away somewhat as a standalone point of focus, with interviewees saying that “ESG for ESG’s sake” is of diminishing importance in a results-driven environment. Against that backdrop, the focus has switched to climate adaptation and ESG investments that drive commercial performance.

“We’ve seen in a very real way that ESG improvements from an energy and utilities cost perspective really drive net operating income,” says a private equity investor. A European institutional investor makes a similar point, saying it “looks at ESG rather as a technical measure to get energy consumption and then the carbon footprint down, more than some sort of aspirational or societal imperative”.

For many interviewees, ESG is less of a talking point simply because it has become integral to real estate strategies. Across Europe, landlords are retrofitting buildings for a warmer climate and monitoring disaster risks, while designers are considering materials, shapes, and natural elements to support cooling urban architecture.

Investor due diligence, meanwhile, is increasingly focused on the viability of coastal locations, extreme heat exposures, and rural risks from woods and forests. Some private equity investors predict that investment in Europe will shift from the south to the north, mitigating the impacts of increasingly frequent heatwaves in the world’s fastest warming continent.

The UN Environment Programme has historically stated that up to 40% of global carbon emissions come from the real estate sector, with 70% produced by building operations and 30% from construction. Not surprisingly, many interviews for this year’s report say that ESG responsibilities remain a priority, despite a shifting political backdrop. Industry leaders are working closely with regulators to strike a balance between ambition and achievability.

Over recent years, the real estate industry has wrestled with challenges of investing in and adopting digital technologies, but the growth of AI has injected a new sense of urgency. With AI impacting how buildings are designed, operated, and experienced, and therefore how value is created, decision makers are gauging how fast and how far the transition will go over the coming year.

Many leaders have two data priorities: first, to unlock stored data held in legacy systems, records, and archives and second, to generate new data through innovations such as Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, smart systems, and digital twins. Companies that marshal clean, connected, and contextualised data will be best placed to put AI to good effect, both in real estate investments and internally. “AI is the engine, data is the fuel, and the destination is better decisions and better returns,” says the CEO of a real estate technology firm.

Many survey respondents report a growing sense of optimism over AI’s potential to drive more efficient operations, with marketing and leasing first in line for transformational impact. Meanwhile, interviewees predict that digital platforms will reshape landlord-tenant relationships, through innovations including automated prospect identification and personalised communications.

Finally, survey respondents say they do not see AI as an arms race. The winners will not be the businesses that buy the most tools but those that successfully combine technology with expertise, human judgement, and high-quality data to transform how they operate.

Institutional investors continue to be drawn to Europe’s world-leading cities. For the sixth consecutive year, London retains its number one position for transaction volumes. Madrid and Paris complete an established top tier. In an uncertain environment, leading cities continue to offer the security of pricing transparency, transaction liquidity, and the confidence of multiple buyer pools.

Outside the top-ranked markets, fast-growing southern European cities are attracting interest, with Milan jumping to fifth position from seventh last year and Barcelona cementing its hold on eighth spot. In Germany, Munich overtakes Berlin to become the country's highest-ranked city for the first time. Central and Eastern Europe's most liquid market is Warsaw, which locks in 12th place overall.

Deep pools of liquidity make cities stand out as investment destinations, but investors are also assessing metrics such as demographic trends, infrastructure build out, housing supply, and long-term competitiveness. In addition, issues around affordability, ageing building stock and climate resilience are shaping perceptions. Cities that can get a grip on these challenges will attract more institutional capital in the years ahead.
